    AI Overview
    El Niño is a climate pattern marked by warmer-than-average sea surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific Ocean. It typically occurs every 2-7 years, often bringing wetter, cooler conditions to the Southern US and warmer, drier conditions to the North. A "Super El Niño" in 2026 may cause stronger global impacts. 
    Key Impacts of El Niño 
    • Global Temperature and Weather: Shifts the Pacific jet stream southward, which causes significant changes in global weather patterns.
    • Wetter Conditions: Enhanced storm activity and increased precipitation often occur in the southern US, Peru, Ecuador, and parts of the Caribbean.
    • Drier Conditions: Drought and extreme heat often strike Indonesia, Australia, and parts of Africa.
    • North American Winter: The southern tier of the U.S. experiences wetter and colder conditions, while northern U.S. states and Canada tend to be warmer and drier than average.
    • Hurricane Activity: Generally increases Pacific hurricane activity while weakening Atlantic hurricanes, according to.
    • Marine Life: Decreases nutrient-rich upwelling along the Pacific coast of South America, which can devastate local fishing industries. 
    2026 Forecast

    BenNollWeather · X
    Meteorologist for The Washington Post
    The latest European model seasonal forecast is calling for a potential Super El Niño to arrive by September. A Super El Niño is informally defined as when temperatures in the Niño 3.4 region in the tropical Pacific exceed 2°C above normal. El Niños historically have led to some of the warmest years on record, including 2024, and this will be no different. Combined with the ongoing trend of global warming, 2026 and 2027 will likely rank among the two warmest years ever recorded in Earth’s modern history. Super El Niños also supercharge extreme weather events around the world, including floods and droughts. In general, expect significant major climate impacts in the next 1.5 years globally. They also bring significantly increased odds of a below-average hurricane season in the Atlantic and a much above-normal season in the eastern Pacific. Stay tuned.

    Duration. How long does El Niño typically last?
    Feedback
    9–12 months
    El Niño typically lasts 9–12 months, and La Niña typically lasts 1–3 years. Both tend to develop during March–June, reach peak intensity during December–April, and then weaken during May–July. However, prolonged El Niño episodes have lasted 2 years, and even as long as 3-4 years.

    Typical Patterns. What are the typical weather patterns during El Niño?
    About this result
    Feedback
    An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
    AI Overview
    El Niño, or the warm phase of the ENSO cycle, typically causes wetter-than-average winters in the Southern U.S. and California due to a strengthened subtropical jet stream. Conversely, it often brings warmer and drier conditions to the Northern U.S. and Canada. Key impacts include increased storminess, flooding in the South, and higher risks of marine heatwaves. 
    Typical Weather Patterns & Impacts (El Niño):
    • Southern U.S. (California to Florida):
      Wetter-than-average conditions (over 80% of events) with increased flooding risk. 
    • Northern U.S. and Canada:
      Warmer and drier conditions, often with lower-than-average snowfall in the Northeast. 
    • Hawaii:
      Reduced precipitation, often leading to drought conditions. 
    • Jet Stream Changes:
      The Pacific jet stream becomes less wavy, focusing storm tracks across the southern U.S. 
    • Marine Impact:
      Marine heatwaves are more common, affecting fish migration and causing algal blooms. 
    Synonyms and Associated Terms: Warm phase of ENSO (El Niño-Southern Oscillation), Oceanic warming event, and El Niño-Southern Oscillation cycle. 
    Note: While El Niño patterns are consistent, they do not guarantee specific weather events, as variations occur, according to.
